title: SRE standards: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview:
This page consolidates Redwood Inference SRE standards for SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and exemplar runbooks. The goal is a consistent, auditable approach to keeping our inference platform available, performant, and cost-effective while minimizing customer impact during incidents and planned changes.

Audience and scope:
- Primary audience: SRE, infra, serving runtime, platform and on-call engineers.
- Scope: hosted, dedicated, and private control plane components (control plane, model-serving API, batching/kvcache, orchestration, autoscaler, and metrics pipelines).

1) SLOs and Error Budgets
Intro:
SLOs quantify acceptable user-visible reliability. Error budgets translate SLOs into operational behavior and rollout constraints. All services must publish SLOs and a corresponding error budget policy.

Required SLOs (examples tuned for inference workloads):
| Service / KPI | Window | Target | Measurement | Notes |
|---------------|--------|--------|-------------|-------|
| Model-serving API: successful request rate | 30d | 99.95% | HTTP 2xx/3xx success for generation endpoints | Excludes scheduled maintenance and documented provider outages |
| Model-serving API: p99 generation latency | 7d | <= 600ms | p99 of end-to-end response time for text-generation requests (small models) | Separate buckets for short and long-sequence workloads |
| Token failure rate (generation error per token) | 30d | <= 0.02% | errors / generated tokens | Important for high-throughput embedding/generation pipelines |
| Embedding throughput (production embedding service) | 7d | >= 95% of committed throughput | measured vs reserved throughput for Dedicated customers |
| Control-plane API availability | 30d | 99.9% | management APIs used by customers to create deployments | often stricter for enterprise customers |

SLO ownership and documentation:
- Each service owner must maintain an SLO doc with objective, measurement method (Prometheus query / metrics id), alerting rules, and dashboard links.
- SLO documents must be reviewed quarterly and before major releases.

Error budget policy (standard playbook):
1. Alerting and reporting:
   - Daily SLO health email to stakeholders if burn > 10% in 7d window.
   - Pager alert when burn rate implies remaining error budget will exhaust within 48 hours (see burn-rate calculation below).
2. Burn thresholds and actions:
   - Green (0-25% of budget consumed in rolling 30d): normal operations.
   - Yellow (25-50%): restrict non-essential changes (delay low-risk but non-critical releases), increase observation cadence.
   - Orange (50-75%): freeze feature rollouts that touch the service, dedicate one reliability-focused engineer to mitigation, start mid-priority incident review.
   - Red (>=75%): immediate release freeze, focus on mitigation and rollback of recent changes; leadership informed; postmortem required within 72 hours of recovery.
3. Burn-rate calculation (example):
   - Remaining budget (%) = (allowed_error_budget - error_so_far) / allowed_error_budget.
   - If observed error rate exceeds SLO by factor X, compute projected time to exhaust as: remaining_budget / (observed_error_rate - SLO_rate).

2) Capacity planning and headroom
Principles:
- Maintain sufficient capacity across GPU pools, serving nodes, and control-plane replicas to meet SLOs while minimizing idle cost.
- Plan for regional failover, burst traffic (30% short-term headroom), and gradual predictable growth.

Process and cadence:
- Monthly capacity review: owners submit utilization metrics, active deployment growth, and forecast for next 90 days.
- Quarterly capacity planning: SRE + Product review forecasts, commit reserved capacity (Dedicated), and plan procurement.
- Change freeze & safety windows: during major traffic events (e.g., enterprise launches) schedule increased headroom and temporarily suspend noncritical autoscaler policies.

Forecasting formula (example):
- baseline_tps = average requests/s over the last 30d
- forecast_tps_90d = baseline_tps * (1 + historical_monthly_growth_rate * 3) * safety_margin
- safety_margin defaults to 1.30 (30% headroom) unless otherwise authorized for cost-savings.

Autoscaling and reservations:
- Autoscaler target: maintain 90th percentile CPU/GPU utilization within target range (GPUs: 60-85% for throughput models; high-util workloads may target tighter windows).
- Dedicated pools: always reserve capacity to meet committed Throughput SLAs with hot standby (10-20% depending on tier).
- Scale testing: every release that modifies batching, kernel selection, or scheduler must run a scale test against the benchmarking suite before rollout to prod.

3) Reliability initiatives and measurement
Quarterly reliability program:
- Each quarter teams propose 1-2 reliability initiatives (RIs) tied to measurable goals: reduce p99 by X ms, reduce incident MTTR by Y minutes, or reduce token-failure rate by Z%.
- RIs tracked in roadmap with owners, milestones, and measurement dashboards.

Examples of RIs:
- KV cache warmup: reduce cold-start latency by pre-warming KV caches for frequently requested prefixes.
- Kernel fallback path: implement fast-fail to quantized kernel when primary kernel causes queuing.
- Observability: add distributed tracing for request fan-out across model shards to speed root cause analysis.

KPIs for reliability program:
- MTTR (mean time to recovery) per severity class.
- Incident frequency per quarter and incident severity distribution.
- Error budget burn rate and percentage of services exceeding thresholds.

4) Incident review standards (blameless postmortems)
Severity classification and initial comms:
- Sev1: customer-impacting outage affecting multiple customers or core functionality. Phone bridge immediate; page to 2 on-call engineers + SRE lead.
- Sev2: partial degradation or single-customer outage with significant impact.
- Sev3: minor degradation or internal issues with low customer impact.

Post-incident expectations:
- Timeline: preliminary incident notes within 4 hours of mitigation; formal postmortem created within 72 hours; final RCA with corrective actions and owner within 14 days.
- Postmortem template (required fields):
  1) Summary — one paragraph overview and customer impact.
  2) Timeline — minute-level timeline of events and actions.
  3) Root cause(s) — technical and contributing factors.
  4) Detection and mitigation — how it was detected, initial mitigations, and when service recovered.
  5) Impact assessment — customers affected, SLOs burned, financial or contractual impact.
  6) Corrective actions — short-term mitigations and long-term fixes with named owners and due dates.
  7) Lessons learned — what changed in process, tooling, or runbooks.

Blameless culture:
- Language matters: focus on system and process improvements. Avoid naming individuals except for owner or action assignee when necessary.

5) Operational tooling and observability stack
Required components (recommended stack):
- Metrics: Prometheus + Thanos (long-term storage).
- Dashboards: Grafana with service-level dashboards (SLO panel, latency distribution, error budget panel).
- Tracing: Tempo (or Jaeger) for request flows across microservices and model shards.
- Logging: Loki for centralized logs, with preserved request IDs and trace correlation.
- Error reporting: Sentry / Honeycomb for structured error capture and sampling.
- Alerting & paging: Alertmanager + PagerDuty integration for on-call routing.
- Incident management: Statuspage for customer-facing incidents and internal incident templates in Confluence.
- CI / perf harness: Benchmarking suite (bench/), k6/locust scripts, and synthetic traffic generators for canary tests.

Tooling standards:
- All alerts must include runbook links and severity guidance.
- Dashboards should have a top-line SLO panel and drilldowns for service, model type, and region.
- Trace sampling should preserve traces for 10% of requests by default, with increased sampling for low-volume or high-error flows.

6) Runbooks: structure and exemplar
Runbook structure (required):
- Title
- Scope and symptoms (when to use)
- Pager and escalation policy
- Quick checks (metrics and dashboards to review)
- Mitigation steps (ordered, reversible where possible)
- Recovery verification (how to confirm service restored)
- Post-incident actions and owner

Exemplar runbook: High tail latency on model-serving-prod
- Scope & when to use: Use when p99 generation latency exceeds 600ms for >5 minutes and error rate remains below SLO but customers report slow responses.
- Pager: page on-call SRE and serving-runtime lead.
- Quick checks:
  1) Check SLO dashboard (Grafana): p50/p95/p99, QS queue depth, GPU utilization, batch size distribution.
  2) Prometheus queries:
     - 100 - (sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="model-serving",status!~"2.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="model-serving"}[5m]))) * 100
     - histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="model-serving"}[5m])) by (le))
  3) Check autoscaler status: kubectl get hpa -n serving | grep model-serving
  4) Check GPU queue length on nodes: xgpu-cli stats or nvidia-smi for node-level metrics.
- Mitigation steps (ordered):
  1) Identify if recent deploy correlates with onset. If so, consider rolling back the most recent canary.
  2) Increase autoscaler max replicas temporarily by 20% and monitor.
     - kubectl scale deployment model-serving --replicas=<current*1.2> -n serving
  3) If queueing on model shards, divert a small percentage of traffic to a lower-latency model variant (fallback): update routing policy via control-plane UI or CLI.
  4) If GPU saturation suspected, reduce batch size as emergency measure (short-term) via feature flag: set BATCH_TARGET=smaller.
  5) If tracing shows hot shard, restart affected pod(s) one-at-a-time: kubectl rollout restart deploy model-serving -n serving --field-selector=metadata.name=<podname>
- Recovery verification:
  - Confirm p99 within target for 10 minutes and request success rate stable.
  - Validate no regression in token-failure rate.
- Post-incident actions:
  - Open incident review, assign RCA owner, list follow-ups (e.g., add autoscaler safety caps, improve canary metrics), and schedule a runbook update.

Runbook ownership and lifecycle:
- Runbooks live in Confluence and must be reviewed every 6 months by the runbook owner.
- Owners are responsible for correcting runbooks after an incident and marking them "verified".

7) Governance and continuous improvement
- Quarterly audit: ensure every critical service has an SLO, a published runbook, and a named owner.
- Postmortem compliance: >95% of Sev1/Sev2 incidents should have a completed postmortem within 14 days.
- Training: run quarterly game days and tabletop exercises to validate runbooks and cross-team coordination.
